headline: Hubbard freed. Witkoff calls Putin a humanitarian.
summary: Russia freed Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, a 74-year-old retired teacher held more than four years on a charge of fighting for Ukraine. Nobody was traded for him. US envoy Steve Witkoff thanked Putin in St. Petersburg and called him a humanitarian. Lawmakers in his own party objected. Vance backed him: the man had just freed a hostage.
cover_answer: Someone who helps people. Plenty say Putin isn't one.
table_question: Should you thank someone for fixing a thing they broke?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Stephen is an American teacher who is 74, and Russia kept him in prison for four years, about as long as you've been at school. On Wednesday Russia let him go. An American helper flew all the way there, said thank you, and now Stephen is on his way home to his family. Doctors will check him over first, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Four years as school years, a thank-you and a plane. Leave the war out.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them four school years, a helper who said thank you and a plane home. The charge, the war and the row over the word stay out unless the child brings them. Expect "why was he in prison?" Russia said he fought for Ukraine. America said that was wrong.

8-12.script: Stephen Hubbard, 74, was captured in Ukraine in 2022; a Russian court gave him nearly seven years. Russia freed him Wednesday, nobody traded back. The US envoy called Putin a humanitarian; some in his own party said it went too far. A handshake after a foul: allowed, and the crowd judges it.
8-12.why: Captured, tried, freed, thanked. Then the handshake.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults keep their own rules, so the script runs the chain: captured, a closed trial, seven years, freed, thanked. The handshake after a foul is the mechanism: allowed, and judged by the crowd. Expect "why did Russia let him go?" The Kremlin says kindness. Trump says he asked.

13-17.script: Is a man a humanitarian for freeing someone he should never have held? Witkoff said so, and lawmakers in his own party objected. That month Trump waived Russia sanctions and bought its diesel. Second: Vance says the words matter less than the homecoming. Is flattery a price, and who pays it?
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a man is going home, and the envoy who got him out flattered the man who jailed him, in the month the US waived sanctions and bought Russian diesel. The script asks whether flattery is a price and who pays it, Hubbard or Ukraine. Expect "so was it a trade?" No swap. The rest is argument.

5-7.a: Someone who helps people. The American helper called the Russian leader one for letting Stephen go. Lots of grown-ups disagreed.

8-12.q: Why did Russia let him go?
8-12.a: Kindness, the Kremlin says. Trump says he asked. No trade.

8-12.q: Why are people cross about a thank-you?
8-12.a: Russia jailed him in the first place. Many found the word too kind.

13-17.q: Did Russia get something for him?
13-17.a: No swap. Trump did waive sanctions and buy Russian diesel, though.

13-17.q: What about the other Americans still held?
13-17.a: Five, their advocates say. Their families ask why not them.

caption:
Someone who helps people. Plenty say Putin isn't one.

Russia freed Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, a 74-year-old retired teacher held more than four years on a charge of fighting for Ukraine. Nobody was traded for him. US envoy Steve Witkoff thanked Putin in St. Petersburg and called him a humanitarian. Lawmakers in his own party objected. Vance backed him: the man had just freed a hostage.
